title: Semi-voiced H ゜— ぱ ぴ ぷ ぺ ぽ

points.shortDescription: The small circle that makes 'p' sounds from the H-row
points.explanation: You've learned the dakuten (゛) — the two strokes that voice a consonant. Now meet the handakuten (゜): a small circle placed at the top right of H-row characters that turns them into 'p' sounds. So は (ha) becomes ぱ (pa), ひ (hi) becomes ぴ (pi), ふ (fu) becomes ぷ (pu), へ (he) becomes ぺ (pe), ほ (ho) becomes ぽ (po). The term 'semi-voiced' or 'half-voiced' (半[はん]濁点[だくてん], handakuten) refers to the fact that 'p' is not fully voiced like 'b', but not unvoiced like 'h' either — it sits in between. The P-row exists only for the H-row; no other row has a handakuten equivalent.
rules: Handakuten (゜) = small circle top-right = H-row becomes P-row.
は→ぱ, ひ→ぴ, ふ→ぷ, へ→ぺ, ほ→ぽ. Only the H-row gets handakuten.
P sounds are unvoiced stops — same lip movement as B sounds but WITHOUT vocal cord vibration.
points.flashcardAnswer: handakuten — small circle; H-row characters become P sounds (ぱぴぷぺぽ)

points.name: ぱ
points.explanation: The syllable ぱ produces a 'pa' sound as in 'pasta' or 'park'. It's the handakuten version of は, transforming the breathy 'h' into a crisp unvoiced 'p'. P sounds in Japanese are unaspirated — same as all Japanese stop consonants — so no puff of air follows the 'p'. ぱ appears mostly in loanwords and expressive words: ぱん (bread — from Portuguese 'pão', one of Japan's oldest loanwords), ぱっと (suddenly / instantly), and ぱちぱち (crackling / clapping sound). Sound-symbolic words (onomatopoeia) in Japanese frequently use P-row characters to convey bright, crisp, or light sensations.
rules: ぱ = は + handakuten; the H-row's breathy 'h' becomes a clean, unaspirated 'p'.
ぱん (bread) is from Portuguese — one of Japan's oldest foreign loanwords, dating to the 16th century.
P-row sounds often appear in onomatopoeia: ぱちぱち (crackling), ぱっと (suddenly), ぴかぴか (shiny).

points.name: ぴ
points.explanation: The syllable ぴ produces a 'pi' sound as in 'peek' or 'piece' — a crisp, bright unvoiced 'p' before the 'ee' vowel. ぴ appears frequently in expressive and onomatopoeic words: ぴかぴか (sparkling / shining brightly — think Pikachu, whose name comes from this word!), ぴったり (exactly fitting / snug), ぴんと (taut / sharp / alert), and ぴよぴよ (the sound of a chick cheeping). The association with brightness, sharpness, and high-pitched sounds makes ぴ a very expressive syllable.
rules: ぴ = ひ + handakuten; breathy 'hi' becomes crisp 'pi'.
ぴかぴか (sparkling) is the origin of Pikachu's name — a fun cultural connection!
P-row sounds, especially ぴ, are associated with brightness, sharpness, and small or delicate things.
points.flashcardAnswer: pi — like the 'pi' in 'peek' (voiced version of ひ with handakuten)

points.name: ぷ
points.explanation: The syllable ぷ combines the unvoiced 'p' stop with the Japanese unrounded 'u' vowel. Keep lips flat after the 'p' — don't round them. ぷ is commonly found in loanwords borrowed from English and other languages: ぷーる (pool), ぷりん (pudding / flan), and in playful onomatopoeia: ぷかぷか (floating leisurely), ぷんぷん (fuming with anger — the visual of steam coming from someone's ears!), and ぷにぷに (soft and squishy). ぷにぷに is a beloved word in Japanese internet culture describing the irresistibly soft texture of baby cheeks and certain foods.
rules: ぷ = ふ + handakuten; the bilabial 'f' of ふ becomes a bilabial stop 'p'.
Both ふ and ぷ use both lips — the difference is that ぷ fully stops the airflow, ふ lets it pass.
ぷ in onomatopoeia often suggests floating, puffing, or soft/squishy textures.

points.name: ぺ
points.explanation: The syllable ぺ produces a 'pe' sound as in 'pep' or 'pepper'. It's the handakuten version of へ — the directional 'h' sound transformed into a crisp 'p'. ぺ appears in common loanwords: ぺん (pen), ぺーじ (page), ぺット (pet — though ペット in katakana is more common), and playful expressions like ぺこぺこ (very hungry / bowing repeatedly). ぺこぺこ is a delightful onomatopoeia for the empty-stomach grumble of hunger, and also describes someone bowing submissively — two very different meanings captured by the same sound-symbolic word.
rules: ぺ = へ + handakuten; the direction particle 'h' sound becomes 'p'.
ぺん (pen) is a loanword — though the katakana form ペン is more common in writing.
ぺこぺこ (hungry / bowing repeatedly) is a fun dual-meaning onomatopoeia.

examples.english: very hungry / bowing repeatedly and submissively

points.name: ぽ
points.explanation: The syllable ぽ is the final P-row character — 'p' before the 'oh' vowel, as in 'poke' or 'pole'. It's the handakuten version of ほ. ぽ appears in fun vocabulary: ぽかぽか (warm and cozy / thwacking sound), ぽっかり (gaping open / floating lightly), ぽかん (dumbfounded / open-mouthed), and the beloved word ぽてと (potato, from the loanword ポテト). Completing the P-row means you've now learned ALL of the basic hiragana — including voiced and semi-voiced characters. That's the entire hiragana syllabary!
rules: ぽ = ほ + handakuten; the warm 'h' sound becomes a crisp 'p'.
ぽかぽか (warm and cozy) is a classic onomatopoeia for a gentle, sunny warmth.
Congratulations — ぽ is the last character in the basic hiragana chart! You've learned them all.

examples.english: gaping open / floating lightly / unexpectedly empty

points.flashcardAnswer: po — like the 'po' in 'poke' (the final hiragana character!)

chapterPractice.prompt: What is the handakuten (゜) and which row does it apply to?
choices: Two strokes that apply to the K-row
A circle that turns H-row into P-row
A circle that turns K-row into G-row
Two strokes that turn S-row into Z-row
chapterPractice.explanation: The handakuten (゜) is the small circle that transforms H-row characters into P sounds: は→ぱ, ひ→ぴ, ふ→ぷ, へ→ぺ, ほ→ぽ. It only applies to the H-row.
ぷ makes the 'pu' sound. It's the handakuten version of ふ. Both use both lips — but ぷ stops the airflow completely (a stop), while ふ lets air pass (a fricative).

chapterPractice.prompt: What does the word ぱん mean, and where does it come from?
chapterPractice.explanation: ぱん (pan) means 'bread' and comes from the Portuguese word 'pão'. Portuguese missionaries and traders introduced bread (and many other things) to Japan in the 16th century, and the word stuck.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does ぴかぴか mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ぴかぴか (pikapika) means 'sparkling' or 'shining brightly'. This is actually the origin of Pikachu's name — the 'pika' refers to the flash of electricity! Onomatopoeia like this is one of the most expressive features of Japanese.
